doc.title: Paquito D'Rivera — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
title: Race among Cuban musicians and in the army
summary: He says race was not a factor among musicians, since the best were Black, though in the army and party most officers and conductors were white.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: When you were coming up as a young musician during this time starting with as a child prodigy performing in the national theater orchestra, and then through your studies at that first conservatory and as you were coming up in the army, was there any recognition of race among the people that you were coming up with?
Was there any sense of separation of people by race?
So that was never a factor?

Not really. The best musicians on that island were the Black people. Well, not only,because Ernesto Lecuona was white and was the representative of the Afro-Cuban composers was a white guy, was Ernesto Lecuona and nobody denied that. And I never feel that in that sense. It’s very simple, if you discriminate against the Black guys, there’s no music. [Both laugh]
Ain’t no music. No, we never feel that. Racist people you can find all over the place.
Was there discrimination, or separation of any kind when you were in the army?

No, not at all. No army. [Both laugh] What can I tell you. Now you mention it, the 90—I ain’t talking about the percentage and all that—the mass majority of the army officers, the high rankings were white. Now that you mention that, I remember. And the party, the center, the Communist party, there was just one Black. And he’s that guy, that like to write music, Romeu. There wasn’t any discrimination, per say, but yes, now that you mention it, I see, there were very few Black officers. Very few, even the conductors of the orchestra or the band was always white. But I don’t think, that in the music, in the music field, I never felt that way.
